Name: Roman/Mediterranean
Modern Definition: The classical Mediterranean world of the Roman Empire: Italy, Greece, Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt and Roman North Africa.
Boundary Notes: Antiquity-only category. Before ~640 AD the Levant/Egypt/N.-Africa Christians are counted HERE, not under Middle East & North Africa (double-count rule).

Name: Western Europe
Modern Definition: Latin/Western Christendom: British Isles, France, Iberia, Italy, the Low Countries, German-speaking lands, Scandinavia.
Boundary Notes: Apportioned split from the source's combined 'Europe' (confidence Low).

Name: Eastern Europe & Russia
Modern Definition: Byzantine and Slavic Orthodox world: the Balkans, Greece, Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and the eastern Slavic lands.
Boundary Notes: Apportioned split from the source's combined 'Europe' (confidence Low).

Name: Middle East & North Africa
Modern Definition: Modern MENA: the Arabian peninsula, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Iran, Egypt and the Maghreb.
Boundary Notes: Independent series intentionally STARTS at year 1000 to avoid double-counting with Roman/Mediterranean in antiquity.

Name: Sub-Saharan Africa
Modern Definition: Africa south of the Sahara, including the Horn and southern Africa.
Boundary Notes: Ethiopian/Nubian Christianity predates 1900 but the series is anchored from 1900 where data is firm.

Name: South Asia
Modern Definition: The Indian subcontinent: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal.
Boundary Notes: Includes the ancient Thomas-Christian communities of Kerala.

Name: East Asia
Modern Definition: China, Japan, Korea, Mongolia and Taiwan.
Boundary Notes: Anchored at 1900 and 2025; intermediate cells deferred to Phase 2.

Name: Southeast Asia
Modern Definition: Mainland and maritime SE Asia: Indochina, Thailand, Myanmar, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia.
Boundary Notes: The Philippines dominates the Christian share.

Name: Latin America
Modern Definition: Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America.
Boundary Notes: Series anchored from 1900; mission-era detail (1492-1600) carried by strands.
